titre: Teaching to understand, exercise judgment and act with others
intro: My academic ambition extends a question that runs through my work as a specialised educator: how can we create conditions in which a person develops their capabilities, exercises judgment and participates in collective action? In public health, this question connects command of knowledge, attention to human experience and responsibility for decisions. I want it to guide my teaching.

vision.titre: Educating people to make sense of situations and take part in them

sections.titre: Knowledge as a capacity to understand and act
paragraphes: University teaching involves more than organising content for students to reproduce. It provides access to demanding knowledge, its history and the approaches through which it can be questioned. I want students to explain how a conclusion was reached, what it supports and what remains uncertain. A concept becomes educationally meaningful when it changes how a situation is understood: identifying a social determinant, making an organisational choice visible or explaining why an intervention affects people differently.

Drawing on Biesta’s distinction between qualification, socialisation and subjectification, I see three connected responsibilities: developing knowledge and capabilities, enabling entry into a community of practice and supporting people in finding their own position within it. Educating competent professionals also means enabling them to question their field’s norms, explain a disagreement and take responsibility for the consequences of their actions.

sections.titre: Pedagogical authority that makes reasoning accessible
paragraphes: My role would be to organise progression, identify expectations and make the criteria for sound reasoning explicit. Student participation rests on this structure. Productive dialogue requires knowledge, preparation and rules that allow arguments to be challenged while respecting people. I want to explain my teaching choices, welcome objections and acknowledge a limit or an error. Academic authority gains legitimacy through responsibility and the possibility of discussing its reasons.

Freire and hooks offer ways of thinking about a relationship in which students’ experience matters and learning engages their relationship with the world. I take from them a responsibility to make room for people’s voices while examining their claims. Lived experience can reveal a decisive question; an empirical proposition then requires appropriate sources and methods. Respecting a person and examining the validity of a statement are part of the same educational task.

pont.titre: Working with people: an ethical continuity translated into teaching
paragraphes: In supporting people with disabilities, I have assessed needs, jointly developed individualised plans and coordinated interventions. Adapted holidays and respite programmes also brought me into contact with different rhythms, communication modes and practical conditions for participation. This experience shapes my attention to what someone seeks to achieve, the resources they draw on and the obstacles that restrict their possibilities.

It also invites me to examine the learning environment: an implicit instruction, an inaccessible resource, a participation rule or a timetable can create barriers. The Human Development Model–Disability Creation Process and Universal Design for Learning offer ways of understanding the interaction between a person and their environment. At university, this attention must respect students as adults, their privacy and their ability to define their own needs. It calls for a pedagogical relationship suited to that setting.

The bridge I want to build rests on self-determination: supporting the capacity to choose and act by providing access to the means to do so. Working with students then involves understandable objectives, feedback, meaningful pedagogical choices and support that can diminish as autonomy develops. The group offers a further resource: learning to seek help, offer it and recognise others’ contributions.
liens: Identify prior knowledge, constraints and barriers to participation without reducing a student to a difficulty.
Clarify expected learning and offer choices of topic or approach where these fit the course requirements.
Provide worked examples, intermediate stages and feedback; gradually withdraw support that is no longer needed.
Connect peer learning, mentoring, teaching teams and university services while respecting roles and confidentiality.

pratique.titre: A developing practice grounded in student support
paragraphes: My four teaching assistant appointments at Université de Montréal provide an initial foundation for this ambition. Student support and the marking of written and oral examinations, documented for ASA 6754 in winter 2026, focus attention on how someone understands a question, uses their knowledge and makes their reasoning visible. These responsibilities take place within the framework established by the course instructors.

I want to develop feedback that helps students rework their understanding: identify a specific achievement, name a priority difficulty and suggest an actionable next step. When a student describes an organisation accurately but explains little about its effects, feedback can invite them to explain the mechanism, consider another hypothesis and examine who is affected. The aim is for a comment to become a resource for subsequent reasoning. Carless and Boud emphasise that using feedback requires learning to make judgments, manage one’s response and take action.

Coordinating the doctoral peer mentoring programme extends this attention to learning conditions. Entering a programme involves understanding its expectations, resources and sometimes implicit conventions. My ambition is to help create an environment in which seeking support is compatible with intellectual rigour and experience circulates among peers. The approach described here guides my development; it is not an evaluation of a course design whose effects I have already measured.

apprendre.titre: Making reasoning, progression and assessment criteria visible
paragraphes: I want to start from the capabilities being developed and use them to design activities and assessment. If the aim is to analyse a health policy, students need opportunities to practise before an examination: define the problem, make assumptions explicit, interpret data and discuss consequences. Constructive alignment gives these activities and their criteria a shared direction.

Active learning interests me when it involves an identifiable intellectual task: explaining, comparing, solving, arguing or revising. Freeman and colleagues’ meta-analysis concerns undergraduate STEM teaching; it supports these approaches within that scope while leaving their adaptation to other contexts to be examined. Retrieval questions, spaced revisiting of key ideas and explanatory correction can also help consolidate knowledge.

I also want assessment to be understandable and usable. Distinguishing practice from assessments that certify achievement gives error and feedback a clear role. An explicit rubric can address problem definition, source quality, argument coherence, consideration of alternatives and attention to consequences. Collective work can include an individual justification to make each person’s learning visible.

avenir.titre: What learning does an interdependent and uncertain society need?

sections.titre: AI: retaining responsibility for one’s reasoning
paragraphes: The rise of generative AI assistants raises a pedagogical question: what can a person actually do when part of the work can be delegated? I want students to learn to choose which tasks to assign to a tool, explain its limits, check its sources and critically examine its outputs. The quality of an assisted text or programme is insufficient to establish its author’s understanding.

PAIRR—peer support and review, AI assistance, then reflection—offers an approach I would like to adapt. Initial personal reasoning, peer discussion, critique of AI suggestions and justification of revisions can make the process visible. Depending on the objective, an oral explanation or an unassisted task can complement assessment. Use rules should be explicit, account for unequal access and protect personal data and confidential work.

sections.titre: Democracy: learning to deliberate while taking evidence seriously
paragraphes: Public health involves debating freedoms, limited resources and unequally distributed risks. Teaching should prepare students to recognise conflicts of values, distinguish scientific uncertainty from political disagreement and listen to people whose experiences differ. I want to develop reasoned deliberation: make reasons accessible, examine decisions’ effects and leave room for challenge. This capacity concerns professional responsibility and democratic life alike.

sections.titre: Health and the living world: connecting scales and consequences
paragraphes: Climate challenges, inequalities and changing health systems require attention to interdependence. A useful response within one service can transfer a burden to families, another sector or the environment. I want to use comparison and systems analysis to help students identify these transfers, their timescales and the people overlooked in a decision. UNESCO’s report on the futures of education provides a framework for reflecting on these collective responsibilities, rather than a single course model to reproduce.

Educating for tomorrow requires sound knowledge and the capacity to revise it. Barnett helps frame education for a future we cannot fully predict: learning to formulate problems, work with reasoned uncertainty and cooperate with other areas of expertise. My ambition is for students to construct a provisional response, explain what would strengthen it and identify when new information warrants changing it.

This ambition also involves the institution: make support accessible, sustain teaching work and examine conditions that enable or prevent participation. I want to contribute to a university that educates people to act together, care for relationships and question the purposes of what they build.

sources.intro: These references support different dimensions of my thinking. Freire, hooks, Biesta and Barnett offer philosophical and theoretical perspectives; UNESCO, CAST and RIPPH provide guiding frameworks. Research on learning and feedback must be read in light of its methods and context. It informs my approach without, by itself, demonstrating the effects of my personal practice.
